utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There are a few matters we have to deal with before the next witness enters the courtroom. First is, as the parties were informed yesterday, that we would deal with some matters we have to deal with before Mr. Donia enters the courtroom. The Chamber considers Robert Donia an expert for the purpose of his anticipated evidence before the Chamber and therefore denies the Defence's request to bar Witness Donia from presenting his evidence with reasons to follow. Any Defence request for delayed cross-examination or recalling of the witness or extended cross-examination will be dealt with after the examination-in-chief of the witness. The Chamber grants the Prosecution motion to add the reports and appendices to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list, reasons to follow, and defers its decision on admission into evidence of the tendered reports and appendices until after the witness has completed his testimony. This concludes this item. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that the Defence intended to raise a matter in relation to cross-examination of Witness Donia so therefore I give you an opportunity first to make any submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. First, I would like to correct something said yesterday on page 15448. My learned friend Mr. Groome said that I received something from my colleague Ivetic that I didn't receive. Actually I did receive, only by my mistake I didn't open it. So for Your Honours it's the same. I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say in all fairness to Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Second, we expected the decision this morning but we also expected the decision to be with reasons regarding of Witness Donia and now we see that it will be -- that the reasons would follow. And we are afraid that if this witness testifies and reasons are given after that, that, again, as many times before, our motion would be moot. So if we anticipate if we are not satisfied with the reasonings, that we would ask for a leave to appeal on this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know whether it would really change anything if the reasons would be there at this moment because an anticipated -- an anticipated request for a certification to appeal would not stop, certainly not automatically stop the hearing of the evidence of Mr. Donia. So in that respect, it may not have any practical consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For us it's not possible to file leave to appeal without reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's perfectly clear but if you would have done so -- if you would have had the reasons, you would have been able to file such a request, then the Prosecution would have an opportunity to respond to that. The Chamber would then decide, which usually takes one, two weeks, at least, and sometimes even considerably more, which would not have stopped us most likely from hearing the evidence of Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, there is also a matter to be raised by the Prosecution. Ms. Bibles, is it you who will deal with that matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- and counsel. Your Honour, as indicated in an e-mail last night, the Prosecution has discovered an error with a document uploaded under P01790 and admitted through Witness Obradovic. The description of the document is correct. However, the ERN, and therefore the document itself, are wrong. We ask the Trial Chamber for permission to replace the document and the English translation of the document into e-court with the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to replace the document uploaded as P1790 by which one? Could you give us the ERN number exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the correct ERN is 0425-8739-0425-8739.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's hereby on the record. There is one other matter. Yesterday, some -- there has been some debate about disclosure, errata and memorandum. The Chamber has not received the memorandum of which Mr. Lukic yesterday said that it changed the report rather than that it clarified the report. Now, we leave it in the hands of the parties at this moment, but if the parties would consider it appropriate that the Chamber would see the memorandum so that we are better able already to anticipate for any further decisions to be taken in that respect, then of course we would need to receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, with your leave I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was misunderstood. It's not that the memoranda changed the report. The memoranda changed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, the memoranda --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- over time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- over time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we received changed memoranda on the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I leave it at this moment. If we don't have it, we can't -- certainly not compare it with previous versions. So we leave it in the hands of the parties, either you further discuss it but then it would be wise that we have it, and if it is not urgent at this moment, then we'll wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll undertake to discuss this with Mr. Lukic over the first break, and if we don't reach resolution, then we will provide the Chamber with both the original memorandum and the revised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other preliminary matters -- I think I hinted already at it yesterday but I would like to put a bit more detail on the record the following. The Chamber would like to remind the Prosecution of the 30th of August, 2013, deadline to submit all remaining 92 bis and 92 quater filings as well as all, except one, bar table motions. Since announcing this deadline on the 19th of July, the Prosecution has only filed two of its announced nine Rule 92 bis motions, four of its announced ten Rule 92 quater motions, and one of its announced seven bar table motions. In order to give the Defence sufficient time to respond to all of these motions, and ensure that they are all decided upon before the end of the Prosecution's case, it is important that the Prosecution files these motions within the time frame agreed to previously. Everyone remains quiet at the Prosecution side. May I take that that you're confident that you will stick to the time limit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do believe that we will be meeting the time limit and there will be some -- some of these motions will be filed today and tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's then hereby again confirmed. I think that we have no other preliminary matters. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one preliminary regarding Dr. Donia. I would move to add a one-page errata to the highlights of assembly report to the 65 ter list. It has been uploaded as 65 ter 30166A. And I would also move to add Dr. Donia's most current CV to the 65 ter list which has been uploaded as 30165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I leave it to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have received the errata. We have looked at it. It's mainly removing doubles from the highlights, some identical portions, and typos, et cetera. It seems to have not much substance. Therefore, leave is granted, the same is true for the updated CV of Mr. Donia. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is one issue I'd like to raise with the Chamber regarding the August 30th deadline. The Prosecution has some pending applications for the addition of witnesses and while we do have the 92 bis applications drafted, it's not our intention to file them until the Chamber enters its decision. So I'm asking for an indication from the Chamber whether we would want those filed by August 30th as well, conditioned upon the Chamber's final determination of our application to add the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll let you know. The Chamber will have to consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that a few drafts are at final stages. Nothing else? Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, I would invite you to make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you'll first be examined by Ms. Bibles. You'll find her to your right and you may be aware that she is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you please state your name, your full name for the record as well as your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Robert J. Donia. I am a retired but formerly professor of history and have also worked in the past in the financial services business.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that the court officer bring the first page of 65 ter 30165 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you prepared a curriculum vitae -- a current curriculum vitae in preparation for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you look at the screen in front of you, can you tell us whether this is the curriculum vitae you prepared?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If the court officer could proceed to the final page, which I believe is 6?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your curriculum vitae indicates that you received a masters and Ph.D. in history from the University of Michigan. Was there an area of history that you focused on in these advanced degrees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I focused in my Ph.D. on the history of southeast Europe, more specifically Yugoslavia and more specifically still Bosnia and Herzegovina, particularly the social and political history of the 19th and 20th centuries and the history of war in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you first visited Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Approximately how many times have you been to Bosnia since 1965?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm not certain of the number. I estimate it at about 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As a Fulbright Scholar in 1974 and 1975, where did you conduct your research?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Principally in Sarajevo, Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also in Zagreb, in Belgrade, Serbia, and also Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you describe your command of Serbo-Croatian or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I speak the language well, not fluently, I would say, but well. I read it with ease and write it haltingly, and particularly have difficulty with reading the Cyrillic handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you describe for us when you began to acquire your language skills?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: 1965, when I was first there, and then resumed again prior to my visit in 1974-75.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us, in the work that you did in the 1970s, what types of documents did you use and review?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I reviewed largely archival documents but also referred to the contemporary press, that is, the press at the time that I was doing research on, and various written accounts by persons from that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What did you notice in that work about the use of language in different types of documents that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I noted the, let's say, vocabulary and lexical practices varied widely depending on the particular context of who was writing them and what institution that person was associated with.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you currently review materials from the region in the original language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Since your academic work in or about the 1970s, you were engaged in a full-time career managing brokerage offices. During that time, did you continue to do some work in history?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In -- yes, I actually began work in the brokerage business, financial services business, in 1981. For the first five, six years of that was able to produce a few articles and also to kind of stay up with the field but then that kind of came to an end and revived again starting in the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you maintained over time involvement with Bosnian academic institutions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in terms of your overall research, has this included current events as well as historical events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I tender 65 ter 30165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1998, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the same objections we had before on this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about the CV at this moment, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm a bit lost. No objections to the CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then P1998 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: On the first three pages of your CV, we learn that you have authored, co-authored or edited a series of books and articles relating to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you describe for the Chamber how you assess the value of a historical source when selecting materials for such works or for reports to Trial Chambers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I have four criteria that I use to assess the value of a historical source. Number one is its source, its origin. Number two is its veracity as verifiable by similar other documents in the same time period that I already considered to be from sources that are reliable. Third is relevance to the topic I'm addressing. And fourth, richness. Richness meaning does this document say something significant about the topic or topics that I am addressing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your most recent work was a selection of excerpts, a book, titled, "From the Republika Srpska Assembly 1991 to 1996." Because this book is similar to one of the reports before the Chamber today, I will ask some questions that apply to both. First question is: How long have you been working with the RS Assembly sessions as a source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Since 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you describe the value of these Assembly session transcripts and minutes, in terms of historical research?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I view them as having great value, in fact, being indispensable sources for learning the motivations, intentions, perspectives and generally understanding of the leaders of the Bosnian Serb national movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your excerpts in the book and in your highlights report are organised thematically. Could you describe for the Chamber how you select materials in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is a somewhat subjective process but I simply go through the transcript and/or minutes of a particular session and identify those parts of it that I think best meet the criterion I have established and then break them down into the eight thematic areas that I've discussed and then present them within each of those areas chronologically.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you work with Assembly sessions, what types of context do you consider in understanding these sessions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think I can address the individual excerpts in particular. I think there are three, let's say, layers of context that are equally important in evaluating these excerpts. First is the specific immediate context, in terms of who spoke the words, in what forum, to whom, what the conversation was about at that point in time, what it succeeded and followed. The second level is the more general one of political and social events, military events going on at the time. So whether it was in peace or war, during a time of discussion of a peace plan or plans for the future. And the third is what I would call the internal context of the movement in question, in this case the Bosnian Serb national movement consisting largely of members of the SDS and their, let's say, codes of language, lexical codes, and the particular meanings that they may assign to terms or significance to particular events and movements.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the court officer bring the first page of 65 ter 30168 to the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to turn attention now to the two reports you've prepared for the Chamber. Is this the first page of the Sarajevo report that you have drafted for this case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You've described the manner in which you select sources. Are there additional factors that you considered in preparing this particular report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In this particular report, I was very interested in the various perceptions of actors but also in establishing a kind of thematic account of the causes, course and consequences of particular actions around the time of and during the siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And what consideration -- did you give additional consideration to the role of the accused in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This report, which is similar to one that I prepared for earlier cases, was designed specifically to be tailored to the role and perceptions, as he expressed them, of the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Does the narrative of this report assume that the reader understands something about Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that the reader will understand something about Bosnia, about Sarajevo, and, for that matter, about the war there in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the introduction to your Sarajevo report, I believe it's pages 2 and 3, you explain that you use a constructive view of nations and nationalistic movements in your report. How did that influence your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Using this framework, which makes essentially national identity a variable rather than a fixed, eternally unmovable part of any person's makeup, means that I do not in this report attribute any -- attribute to ethnicity any particular action in and of itself. It is not a motivation. It might become a motivation in conjunction with something else. And then second, it means that I do not either give particular credit -- credulity, nor do I discount the credulity of any statement depending on the ethnicity or national identity of the person who made it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe for us the organisation of the end notes to this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The end notes are the text of the B/C/S original of statements made by individuals or in publications, and they reflect the original of the text solely for the purpose of those who are reading B/C/S, who read B/C/S and are trying to, let's say, assess the accuracy of the translation and the language that was used in the original B/C/S, and they come at the very end of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you describe how the appendices are to be used in conjunction with this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There are several appendices that -- to the report. They simply give some visual, in the case of maps, or numerical substance to what I've described in the text itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the court officer bring 65 ter 30167 to our screens?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And while this is coming to our screens, could you describe whether the appendices is comprised of five maps and a table?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would ask that both 30167 and 30168 be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 30168 will be MFI P1999. And 30167 will be Exhibit -- MFI P2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will decide later on admission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the court officer now bring 65 ter 30166 to the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first page of the report that I have called the highlights of deliberations in the Republika Srpska Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Just briefly, could you describe how the excerpts are organised in terms of topic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. They are, and I think the topics are listed on the second page of the report, again broken into eight different themes or topics within which there is a chronological presentation of excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the court officer could bring up in English first page 111 and in B/C/S page 152?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With respect to highlights 258 and then 259, which is on the next page of both, is there a correction that you would like to make to the date?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I provided the wrong date on those two sessions. It was not 12 May of 1992 but, I believe, 15 to 16 May -- or July of that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In preparation for your testimony, did you prepare -- review and prepare a list of corrections?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the court officer could bring 65 ter 30166A to our screens?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When you look at the screen, is this the one-page errata that you have prepared?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would ask that both 30166A and 30166 be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 30166 will be MFI P2001, and 65 ter number 30166A will be MFI P2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And will keep that status for the time being. Could I seek clarification? Mr. Donia, you said you provided the wrong date on the two sessions, that is, both the 20th session, which in items 258 and 259 is the 12th of May, 1992. And you said, "but I believe 15 to 16 May or July." That sounds like Easter or Christmas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is July, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 15 to 16 July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I frankly can't recall whether it's 15 to 16 or 16 to 17 July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a two-day session in July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Next area of discussion will involve the six strategic objectives as of 12 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the court officer bring 65 ter 03432 to our screens?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us what we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. In the left-hand column starting about a third, a quarter, of the way down, we are looking at, at least on my screen, a B/C/S version of the English that's appeared now on the right side which was published in the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska on November -- in November of 1993. It refers, however, to an action taken on 12 May 1992, and then proceeds to list the strategic objectives or priorities of the Serb people in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you read for us the first strategic objective?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, the demarcation of the state as separate from the other two national communities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us what significance, if any, there is to the publication of the objectives in this gazette?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The documentary minutes and transcript of the 16th session on the 12th of May do not reflect that this set of strategic objectives were formally adopted by the Assembly. This represents, then, the actual publication which would mean they are officially recognised by the state as normative without actually reporting further documentation that they were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Going back to the first strategic objective, is the meaning of this first stated goal, regarding whether it's a state or political boundary or a human-based boundary, obvious from a literal reading in the original language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: To me, it is not. It is close, but the fact of the matter is that the notion here kind of mixes two kinds of separation, one being a demarcation of the state, which is normally thought of as simply drawing a border on a map, and the second is one pertaining to separation from national communities. To me it's ambiguous exactly what is meant in this particular objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As a historian, what did you look to to understand the intent and meaning of this stated goal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I looked at the language used to describe the goal by those people who believed that it had been adopted on the 12th of May in -- and they recited these strategic objectives, various people did, many times, in the course of the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions, so I looked to those excerpts to better understand what that first strategic objective meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Before we go to some of those sources, Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 03432.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 03432 will be Exhibit P2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2003 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now turning to some of the sources that you looked to in determining the meaning behind this objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the court officer bring -- I believe it became P2001, the highlights report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for that, could I ask you one question, Mr. Donia? If you look at comments of people on these six strategic objectives, you told us that that would assist you in understanding the meaning of it. Now, important texts are now and then also abused by persons who use those texts to try to find support for their own opinions rather than to express what the authors of that text may have meant. This is said about important, for example, religious documents like the Bible. Could you tell us how you can distinguish between abuse and -- of the text and clarification of a text in later words spoken by persons who may not be the authors of the text itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, for the question. I absolutely agree that this or any text can be abused by people who would give it a meaning and serve a purpose that it was not actually written to serve. However, it's important, I think, to look at the context in which a particular proposal was made and adopted, and the way that people understood it. And this is something that's done, for example, all the time in, say, looking at the debates in the Security Council before a resolution is adopted and looking at the debate, for example, in any legislative body as a measure is introduced and then passed or defeated. So it's a -- quite a different exercise really in trying, without presuppositions, to go in and determine the meaning of that in the sense of the intent of its drafters and promulgators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could turn to in English, page 11, and then 12, in the English version, and then page 13 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm directing your attention first to highlight 14. Is this one of the sources that you consulted in your inquiry on this point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the 14th highlight is not yet visible in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I think it's e-court page 13, if that helps. I'll note that in the English version, the second part of this excerpt is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: But before we turn to that, I'll ask if you could briefly explain the context in which this statement was made on the 18th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: On that date, the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats reached an agreement in principle, which is known as the Lisbon Agreement or the Cutileiro Agreement. This was an agreement in principle only. It was not signed nor finalised by any of the parties, but it is to this agreement in principle that the -- Mr. Krajisnik is reacting at the 11th session, which was largely devoted to discussion of that plan. And he is therefore trying to position that agreement in the context of the values that the Bosnian Serb movement has adopted. And of course in the first sentence here, he endorses the fundamental notion of a division according to ethnic principles, and then in the second paragraph, which as you noted is on the next page, he proposes that that principle be implemented now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So what did you gather from this excerpt about the separation goal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It seems to me evidence that the separation goal was held by the key leaders of the Bosnian Serb movement well before the actual adoption of the -- or the discussion and putative adoption of the goals on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then moving to the next excerpt, number 15 - just checking, I believe all of this is depicted on both screens here - in what context now on the 27th of March is this statement made?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is a statement made several Assembly sessions later, at a time when the -- Karadzic and the other leaders are figuring out ways to get their strategic plans implemented as soon as possible, and it is in this context then that Karadzic speaks about the, let's say, fundamentality of the goal, its foundational character, and asserts that it was, in fact, sort of a part of the very Serb essence for some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you look sometimes at quotes made later in time for their retrospective view?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that those are -- can be very revealing. They have to sometimes be treated with a certain caution because people don't always remember exactly what they were thinking or saying previously, but nonetheless, can have great value in illuminating the situation in prior times.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in that vein, if we could go to e-court page 23 in English and e-court page 31 in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We are looking down the road now at 1944. I'd like to direct your attention to highlight 46. Could you describe for us the context of this statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we are dealing with 1994, hopefully, not 1944. But in this -- this is one of many reiterations that Karadzic makes in Bosnian Assembly sessions in which he's trying to impart the essence of the -- usually the first strategic goal and in which he very clearly here states that it is a human boundary that is to be established by whatever means are required.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Based on your full rigorous examination in this area of the meaning of the first strategic goal, what type of separation, in your examination, is meant by the first objective?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think looking at the various reiterations and the iteration itself, one can conclude that what was intended here was both complete political separation, separation of polities by a border, and coeternally the same border would serve as a human separator between, on the one side, Serbs and, on the other side, Croats and Muslims or others.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock and I can advise the Chamber that we are right on schedule with this examination. I note that this is -- we are approaching a time for a break and this would be an appropriate time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take the break now. Could I first ask the usher to escort Mr. Donia out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile I use the time for dealing with protective measures for Witness RM021. On the 5th of December of last year, the Prosecution sought to have the protective measures of pseudonym and closed session granted to witness RM021 in Brdjanin rescinded. The Chamber granted this request in its decision on the 9th motion to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis which was issued on the 18th of July. In that decision, the Chamber denied the admission of Witness RM021's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, and on the 19th of July, the Prosecution made an oral application to change the 92 bis motion into a 92 ter motion and stated that it was likely that the witness would request to have his protective measures reinstated for his appearance in court. The Chamber invites the Prosecution to make submissions as a matter of urgency on the reasons behind reinstating the protective measures for Witness RM021 given the witness is due to testify on Monday, the 26th of August of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. D'Ascoli will be making those submissions. Would you like me to have her here at the beginning of the next session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that would be a good idea so that we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, apologies for dealing with other matters when you're coming into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles will now continue her examination-in-chief. May I take it that you need another 45 minutes, Ms. Bibles? It was scheduled for one hour and a half, if I'm not -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I should finish up within the next 45 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us your understanding of the significance of the first strategic goal with respect to the overall Bosnian Serb nationalist movement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I think this first goal marked a transition with within the Bosnian Serb movement from basing claims upon their habitation-based claims, that is, lands on which Serbs live or lived in -- and may have been removed by virtue of alleged genocide in the Second World War, and movement to claims which were strategic in character and essentially trumped any considerations of residence or habitation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As we've explored how you research and identify the excerpts, you've indicated that one level of understanding must be appreciating the internal context or lexicon used by the Bosnian Serb leadership. How do you do this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The one thing that works every time is to simply go through an awful lot of the documentation and reports and note patterns of usage. Often, there will be some sort of official policy annunciated about terms that should be used or should not be used in particular contexts, but I would say that's not always the case when searching for these lexical conventions and usage conventions that I'm speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were there words or phrases used by the Bosnian Serb nationalistic movement which had meanings beyond the literal reading?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is the word "Turk" one of these terms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe the history of the word and then how it was used from 1992 through 1995 in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In widespread usage in Europe and really all over the world, the term was used, of course, in reference to the inhabitants or citizens of the Republic of Turkey in the 20th century. It was also used to refer to the Ottoman Empire, in place of the word Ottoman, and as such had really no pejorative connotations for a long time. But in the course of the 20th century, and possibly even a little bit before, it began to be used by those peoples who had lived under the Ottoman Empire pejoratively to describe the empire that they regarded as having oppressed them in the 19th century and before. So that by the time the -- let's say the elections of 1990 came along, the term "Turk" had acquired severe pejorative connotations and Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats began to use it to refer to the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that then brought with it the negative connotations of the Ottoman Empire's behaviour toward other peoples and also associated the term with, broadly speaking, Turkish ambitions which they believed existed in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So when the phrase was used either by the leadership or on the street from 1992 to 1995 in Bosnia by a Bosnian Serb, what was the connotation or the meaning behind that word?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, it was a pejorative term that implied enemy, an enemy that posed a direct and immediate threat to the very existence of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In reviewing the Assembly sessions, did you also make observations regarding the use of the word "genocide"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what observations you made?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In looking at the use of the word "genocide" in the course of these Assembly sessions, I noted anecdotally at first that the term was used almost exclusively in reference to deeds committed against Serbs by members of other peoples, and only rarely was it used in reference to deeds committed by Serbs against others. So I looked at the excerpts report that is before us, highlights report, and noted that just judging the usage of the term, it occurred 12 times in reference to deeds against Serbs and only twice that I was able to find in deeds committed that -- that could be or potentially were committed by Serbs. I did a further examination of 44 of the sessions which were searchable and found that that numerical disproportionality even is greater when looking at that broader set of sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What significance, if any, did you draw from that observation in reviewing the Assembly sessions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the -- by consensus of the speakers in the Assembly session, that genocide was a dirty word that Serbs were not capable of engaging in and had not engaged in, and therefore, it should not be employed in the discussions that were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the court officer bring page -- well, out of P2001 in e-court, page 78 in the English, and page 108 in the B/C/S to our screens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I meanwhile ask a question to Mr. Donia. Mr. Donia, you say there was a disproportionate use of the word "genocide," it mainly being used in relation to what happened to the Serbs rather than what Serbs would have done. Now, whether it's disproportionate, would you agree with me that that depends on what the reality would have been? If the facts were such that the acts referred to were mainly committed against Serbs, would it then be disproportionate to use it more often in that context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly would, if the facts, in fact, bore that out. The facts, of course, are contested widely by historians and, for that matter, populists, popular writers, and the -- I would not say that would be true of the prospect of genocide being committed going forward. That might not actually create a disproportionate use of the term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you this question because you referred to the disproportionateness only in numerical terms, where it only becomes disproportionate if you look at the fact as well, not only at the numerical use of the term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could also become disproportional simply by a decision of the leading lights in any given movement, to make this a central part of their, say, ideological or propaganda appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So numbers in itself do not -- are not the key to whether it's disproportionate. That is just numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they were just numbers, yes, they could be very important, however, in determining that but might not be at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Based on your review and experience, looking at this issue, do you have an opinion as to the significance of the disparity in those numbers in this instance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I think the significance is that the Serbs, Serb nationalists, believed that it was beyond the realm of their character, their nature, to engage in genocide, and therefore could not possibly have committed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I would like to turn to excerpt 182. We are looking at the end of 182 in the English version. We may need to go backwards in the B/C/S version. If in the B/C/S version we could, then, go to the next page, the quote we are looking at is actually on the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You've explained that there were, in the excerpts, only two citations in which the word "genocide" was used in conjunction with possibility of Bosnian Serb action. Are we looking at one of those two quotes here in highlight 182?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, in the last sentence, last paragraph of the item that you've identified, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Who is speaking in this excerpt?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: General Mladic is speaking here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And what date is this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is the 12th of May, 1992, at the 16th session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe the context in which this statement is made?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: General Mladic has just prior to this made a number of statements expressing his concern or alarm that the leaders of the -- civilian leaders of the movement were formulating goals that couldn't possibly be achieved by those who were supposed to implement them. And he repeatedly, in fact, emphasises the point that the army can only do so much and that there is a limited possibility of achieving this, both because he felt that Serbs could not rule over areas where no Serbs lived, and also because they didn't have the military wherewithal to accomplish it. And so this stands out to me as a particularly harsh warning against taking these actions and fearful of the consequences of it, so that he is really using the word here almost for its shock value because it just doesn't appear in very many other contexts with this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say a warning, a warning to the political leadership, is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a warning to -- yes, to all Serbs, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In reviewing this excerpt in the context in which you have the backdrop, what do you understand the accused to be saying when he uses the words: "People, that would be genocide"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, he is assigning this term, which I -- again has a certain shock value, to certain activities that he either believed were going on or believed might go on through the -- this overly ambitious programme that the leadership was advocating.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you explain to us, in this lexicon or this manner of using some terms or not using terms, what benefit, if any, the Bosnian Serb nationalist leadership gained from this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, in their use of the term, they certainly gained a broad consensus and were able to persuade others outside the movement that the Bosnian Serbs had suffered a great deal in the past from this existential threat and furthermore that it would revive or could revive and be re-enacted in the present or near future.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Given the nature of the Assembly sessions, are there some sessions in which it is more helpful in understanding the speakers, their actions, their intent, to review the entire Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there are. Of course, I'd like to say they are all critical but I think that there are a few sessions which -- these would be the sessions at which I had difficulty drawing just a few excerpts from, that are really very powerful explainers of the situation or attitudes involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, then, going back to the strategic objectives, with the overall or overarching goal of the first strategic objective in mind, what was the nature of the remaining strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The remaining five objectives were all specifically geographical in character, defining the territory on which or within which the first goal should be achieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, with that in mind, we'd turn to the map book, P178, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Dr. Donia, I'm going to ask you to go through the strategic goals with the map in mind. We will go through them one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If I could have just a moment, Your Honour. If we could turn to the next map, that must be page 7 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the second strategic goal, could you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The second strategic goal was to create a corridor from east to west, that is, from Semberija area to the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you tell us whether, in 1991, there were multi-ethnic communities in this corridor region?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The most multi-ethnic area of the projected corridor was the areas to the east, to the right as we are looking at the map. The one municipality which was Bijeljina, sort of right at the corner, right at the north-east corner of Bosnia, had a Serb absolute majority of about 59 per cent. The next five municipalities going to the left or to the west either had no majority group, no absolute majority group, or had a Croat majority. So -- and one actually had a -- that was Brcko had a Muslim plurality. And within those municipalities there was a great deal of mixed population. So the multi-ethnicity was mainly in the eastern part of this and became more solidly Serb as one moved west.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you describe for us strategic goal number 3?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Third strategic goal was to establish a corridor in the Drina Valley, that is, to eliminate the Drina as a state boundary between Serb lands. That then pertained to the area on the very east side of Bosnia, where the Drina River had essentially been the definition of the boundary between the Serb -- between the Republic of Serbia on the right side and Bosnia on the left side. And, again, those areas with the exception of Bijeljina had -- the next four municipalities going down had a Muslim plurality or absolute majority, thus again suggesting that this strategic goal was overriding the habitation-based standards for land claims.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you describe for us the fourth strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The fourth one is to me the -- maybe the most difficult to explain, although it's very straightforward in text. The fourth goal is to establish a border on the Una and Neretva rivers. Now, those two rivers are marked on this map in blue and the -- I think they deserve just a word of explanation as to what they mean. The Una River starts, as you can see in the highlands right on the border between Croatia and Bosnia and flows due north, then turns at the city of Bihac, approximately, to the north-east and then eventually flows into the Sava River at the village of Jasenovac where the blue line ends here. What that boundary does is to draw a specific line which demarks on the northwestern side two almost exclusively Muslim municipalities, that is, Velika Kladusa and forgetting the name of the other, and then half, approximately half of two other municipalities which also have substantial Muslim populations but less overwhelmingly so. Consequently, the idea there was to create a -- basically an enclave which the Serb strategic aims did not penetrate into but they penetrated right to the boundary of it including some lands that were then inhabited by Muslims. The second river that's mentioned here is the Neretva. The Neretva starts again in the highlands of Western Herzegovina, flows northwest and then kind of turns around, flows south to -- south and southwest to the Adriatic Sea and goes significantly right through the city of Mostar. And based on the ethnic distribution in that area, one can readily see that this border was to serve as a border between Croat-inhabited lands to the left of the river looking at the map, and areas of Serb and Muslim mixed population, in some cases more purely Serb, to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Skipping the fifth goal for the moment, could you describe for us the sixth strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The sixth goal was access to the sea for the Republika Srpska, something which existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself only in that small area where it says access to the sea, looks like an anvil, upside-down anvil. So this was to take some sort of territory that would grant Republika Srpska an immediate outlet to the sea, to the Adriatic Sea.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. We can close the map book at this point. In your Sarajevo report - and just for reference pages 16 to 20 in both the English and B/C/S - you describe the setting, origins and growth of Sarajevo. We won't go into those details but I would ask you to describe for the Chamber what the fifth strategic objective meant for the future of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Sarajevo being a very ethnically mixed city in most of its areas, this goal meant that there would have to be considerable separation, movement of peoples from their current homes to some other location, and the creation then also of two separate political regimes, one which was preserved or supposed to be Serb and one which would be Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Before we turn to the concrete aspects of implementing these objectives, could you tell us whether there were critical points in time that marked defining moments in the direction of the Bosnian Serb nationalistic leadership to these objectives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. And I'll identify three early in the movement but recognise that others might identify other high points. But to me, the most significant high points in the movement, the Bosnian Serb national movement, are, first of all, the elections of November 18, 1992 -- 1990, which brought the three national parties to power and basically banished the communist authorities, and indicated that ethnicity was now politically salient in the political life of the republic. Second would be the 15th of October, 1991, a point at which, owing to the decisions of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serb party essentially gave up on the idea of remaining in Yugoslavia, that all of Bosnia would remain in Yugoslavia, and instead started to move toward defining strategies for creating a state of their own and a takeover, seizure of power, in parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to realise that state. Those -- and then the third one would be, in my view, the adoption of the six strategic goals which moved this whole territorial process from one based on residence and individual municipalities to the broader strategic goals that were articulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Let's direct attention to the 15 October 1991 date. Was there a public forum in which these issues were discussed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The 8th session of the Bosnian parliament which began, I believe, on the 10th or 11th of October and concluded in the early morning hours of the 15th of October, was the forum in which these issues were debated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar a speech given by Radovan Karadzic on the 15th of October, 1991, in that venue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Again this is presumably in the very early morning hours of the 15th, after a very long session. He did give a -- what has turned out to be a memorable speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, turn now to 65 ter 22722A, which is a ten-minute video. However, at this time I would ask Ms. Stewart to play just a segment of this video from 9 minutes 29 seconds to 9 minutes 56 seconds. It is my understanding that the transcription has been provided to the booths.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have a page reference? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, and my apologies. That reference would be page 4 of 4 in the English version, and I believe the end of page 3 of 4 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we have to play it twice. First time without, second time with, interpretation. That's a technical matter, Mr. Donia. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we stop? I thought that when it was played for the second time, that we were to receive the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not find it on page 4 but now we have found it on page 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like it to be played for the first time again or are you ready when it's replayed to provide us with the translation -- the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are ready. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could it be played now second time with interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Radovan Karadzic: It is not good what you are doing. This is the road that you want to take Bosnia-Herzegovina to. The same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia-Herzegovina to hell and Muslim people to possible extinction because the Muslim people will not be able to defend themselves if it comes to war here. Please ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Has Radovan Karadzic previously spoken about the Muslim population in Bosnia in this manner publicly before this time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, in public.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: From the date of this speech until the outbreak of war, could you briefly describe the actions of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They began immediately on this same day, in the evening, to plan steps to move closer to creation of a Bosnian Serb state within Bosnia. They subsequently convened a separate Bosnian Serb Assembly, the transcripts of which we are dealing with here, and convened it for the first time on the 24th of October in 1991. They then held a plebiscite on an issue which they believed would authorise them to proceed with forming a state. And they then engaged in some planning to differentiate, within municipalities, between Serb and non-Serb areas and mobilise local SDS members to take measures to take power in the Serbian parts of those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: By reference only, in pages 31 to 32 of your Sarajevo report, you describe the SDS introduction of Variant A and B strategies to the municipality structure. Could you describe how this fit into the political development of the Bosnian Serb nationalistic movement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It fit in as a specific plan which gave very detailed instructions to lower level municipal -- or municipal leaders of the SDS which was very much in accord with a resolution that they had passed at the Assembly session just seven days before. So it was a further implementation of the planning process in advance of whatever was going to follow, either an actual takeover or the creation of a Serb state within -- through diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In terms of Sarajevo, could you briefly describe how the municipality strategy was implemented?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The -- Sarajevo was a bit different from many other areas of the country, in that fairly early in the process, right around the, say January, February, of 1992, the Bosnian Serb leaders created a new municipality, which actually had been an existing one some decades before, called Rajlovac, and rearranged all the boundaries of the -- or much of the boundaries of the existing municipalities to sort of correspond with the creation of that new Rajlovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We've largely discussed the political and ideological development of the rise of the Bosnian Serb nationalistic agenda. Could you briefly describe the role played in this by Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe the role played in the political and ideological development, the rise of the SDS and Bosnian Serb nationalistic agenda by Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was elected president of the party of the SDS at its founding Assembly in July of 1990, and led the party in the election campaign prior to the elections of November 18th. Probably was their principal ideological spokesman but not necessarily innovator of ideology, and then continued to lead the party while never holding any official office within the Bosnian government structure after the elections right up until the outbreak of war -- and, well, and further after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In highlight 281, Radovan Karadzic describes that he asked for Mladic and got him. Overall, could you tell us how well the accused, Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Nikola Koljevic got along?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Based on discussions within the Bosnian Serb Assembly and some additional press accounts outside of it, I would say that the top three civilian leaders of the Bosnian Serb movement got along very well. That would be Nikola Koljevic, who was a professor of English at the University of Sarajevo and a long-time friend of Karadzic, and Momcilo Krajisnik, also a long-term -- long-time friend of Karadzic. That level of cohesiveness did not exist with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Generally, how did they work together during the conduct of the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the three of the political leaders with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the -- I think the three political leaders very often met informally and sort of scripted what was going to happen in the various decision-making bodies. And they acted as civilian leaders of a military organisation, believed that it was their duty to set goals, to prescribe policies, and that it was General Mladic's duty to carry them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, in fact, through the conduct of the war, did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it did, in the main. There was a great deal of, let's say, heat generated between them about these policies, and in particular in certain Assembly sessions these clashes became quite pronounced. But looking at the overall policy implementation in general, General Mladic did carry out those policies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We turn our attention finally to the implementation of the strategic goals. Ratko Mladic officially, you note in your report, officially first had a role in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 25th of April, 1992. In terms of implementing these six strategic goals, what role did Ratko Mladic have in making these happen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, he had the overwhelming burden of responsibility for implementing them. I wouldn't say exclusively because there were other security forces that were tasked to implement parts of these things, but as commander of the army, or its Chief of Staff, General Staff, it was to him that they turned to implement the actual strategic goals that had been laid out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you seen any indication that, as of the 12th of May, 1992, that Ratko Mladic had any misunderstanding as to what was expected of him as commander of these forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I don't see any -- I don't have any instances or evidence that he did not understand what those orders were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is there a relationship between the six strategic objectives and the military directives that were issued during the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The military objectives, in particular number 3 through 7, were the specific means by which the strategic goals were achieved or implemented by the -- both the civilian and the military leaders. There are a couple of exceptions, I believe, when the specific operation was to go beyond some of the boundaries laid out in the six strategic goals. For example, for the purpose of creating disruption behind the lines of the enemy. Things like that. But by and large, those goals were focused on -- or the directives were focused on reaching the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Ratko Mladic addressed several of the Assembly sessions. I'd like to focus on the 37th Assembly session in January of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: While I ask the court officer to bring 65 ter 2388, e-court page 49 in English and 36 in the original to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll ask if you could briefly describe the context for this time period.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The 37th session was held immediately after the Vance-Owen Peace Plan had been presented to all parties in, I believe it was Geneva and the Assembly was debating whether this would -- is something that ought to be accepted by the Bosnian Serbs or whether they ought to accept it or whether they should reject it and seek further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention on the English version, we see a 35 -- a number 35 in the middle of the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They are both in English. Now the B/C/S appears.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe actually in the original language we will need to go to the next page, just above the 35. I'm sorry, it was the page before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just above 35 means the last part of 34.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The last part of 34, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the last line before the 35, first, can you tell us who is speaking here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I cannot actually. It's not clear to -- I don't have that page in front of me when the speech begins.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the quotation, "my concern is not that they create a state, my concern is to have them vanish completely," during the session?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, actually this speech was delivered by General Mladic at that session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And when he indicates that his concern is to have them vanish completely, who is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It's the enemy, and it isn't really clear whether that is Muslims, Croats, all Muslims and Croats, or just one of the groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Finally, in your review of the Assembly sessions, as you go through the conduct of the war, could you characterise Ratko Mladic's dedication to the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think in time, he became very dedicated to them, and said so on several occasions. That represented, in the sense, a development from his approach or his words at the 16th Assembly on the 12th of May in which he expressed these reservations about the scope of them while still embracing three of the concepts that were inherent in the goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And to highlight, what were the three concepts that he embraced?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: At the 12th -- on the 12th of May he spoke forcefully in favour of delineation, establishing boundary, and also about the importance of the corridor, the east-west corridor, and he also spoke in favour of stronger military action in the Sarajevo theatre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, approximately 50 minutes ago, you conveyed to us that were you confident that you would finish in 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I am now finished. I apologise for that, I am apparently a tad rusty in estimating my time, but I am now finished with direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I should have left it to you to say that instead of reminding you of the times.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: One final matter, Your Honour. I would tender 2272A, which is the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you've played only half a minute, where it is by far longer. I do understand approximately nine minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It is the full -- what we played was the end of the speech of Radovan Karadzic. The ten-minute segment is the entire speech that Radovan Karadzic made at that occasion which I would include primarily for fairness and context to the words spoken at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you consider it to be more fair to have the whole ten minutes for context?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I leave it to the Prosecution, whatever they deem necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no objection against the whole ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, the number of the video, the entire video under that number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 22722A will be Exhibit P2004, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2004 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, there would be approximately five minutes left before the break. Would you prefer to take the break now and then start your cross-examination or would you rather start your cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we first have a break, then I can organise myself during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take the break. Yes, Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one additional matter. The B/C/S translation for Dr. Donia's CV, which is P1998, has now been uploaded into e-court under a doc ID number 0686-0156-B/C/S. I request -- the Prosecution requests that the court officer be asked to link the translation with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The court officer is hereby instructed to attach it to the -- and the Chamber should not have admitted it without a translation. Could the parties always, if they submit any document for admission, clearly announce if there is no translation. Then we would first like Mr. Donia to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we will resume at ten minutes past mid-day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to apologise to the Prosecution where I made it look more urgent than it really is when I said the witness concerned would give his testimony on 26th. He's only the third witness next week. But despite that, Ms. D'Ascoli, if you could address the matter and I do not know whether you want to do it in open session or in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: In private session, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. You're excused, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic and you'll find him to your left. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand that for you it's the same if I ask you in either B/C/S or English language and it's much easier for me to continue in B/C/S but you'll probably follow in English?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yeah, I would prefer that you -- well, if -- you can proceed as you wish. I'll get it one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know that you can choose either to listen to the B/C/S or the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if I listen to the English I get a little bit of the benefit of both so I'd like to listen to the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you're already used to this. You got used to it in the previous trials. However, since this is a different trial, we will have to go through this exercise, if you will, so I'm going to ask you something about the field that you provided your expert opinion in here. First of all, for the transcript, let us establish that you are not a political scientist and that you do not have any training in that field.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am not a political scientist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're not an anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am not an anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're not a sociologist or a psychologist or a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, you were not trained in the field of demography?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct, I have not been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're not a statistician either, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm not a statistician. I have had some training in statistics but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're not a lawyer, especially not an expert in constitutional law, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you're not a military expert either?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to say that we received your CV on the 12th of August, 2013, and tomorrow we will probably have to go back to certain aspects of it.
