However, today, I'm just going to ask you -- actually, you worked for Merrill Lynch for the longest period of time from '81 to 2000; isn't that right? If we look at your career?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked for this company full time; isn't that correct? Full working hours?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a salary as a historian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: As a professor of history and instructor of history, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many years would that be, if we look at your entire career?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know. Around six or seven, perhaps, altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you're often asked and I'm going to deal with this just very briefly, it's actually about your foundation that you established in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As you explained, there is this play of words. In Donji Vakuf, you established the Donia Foundation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the best explanation of it I've heard anyone make, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who are the beneficiaries of this foundation, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There are none. The foundation doesn't exist anymore. It did have beneficiaries in the past or, let's say, recipients of the distributions from it. Those included the University of Michigan, the St. Lawrence University, and a small NGO which was -- existed in the US but its mission was to bring together business people in Bosnia in the late 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So was one of the functions of this foundation to be a religious school or is that not the case? Because we find the word "Vakuf" in the name of the foundation, and that is a Muslim religious school, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is, and the function of the foundation had nothing to do with any religious school of any persuasion, other than the fact, if one could call St. Lawrence University by virtue of its name a Christian university, then perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to move on to a completely different topic and I'm going to ask you the following. You read the indictment against General Mladic, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One of your papers in this case is precisely based on the indictment and is used as support to the indictment, and these are these excerpts from the sessions of the Assembly of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, they could be used that way. I'm assuming that was one of the purposes for which I was asked to bring the report together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, in the previous trials, and I must note that I observed that too, very often you rely on newspapers, newspaper articles, books, memoirs. Would you agree that these are primarily books of memoirs and newspapers that write about other documents and that they are therefore secondary sources?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I don't really use -- accept the designation or distinction between primary and secondary sources anymore and, frankly, most historians do not, have not probably for 50 years. So I would say the character of those writings and memoirs that I have -- and documents that I've used is very diverse. Some of them are in archives. Some of them are in newspapers. Some of them are in secondary works of -- in the sense that they are produced by a publisher and not -- I'm not looking at the immediate original text. So they are very diverse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So am I understanding you correctly, namely that you did not distinguish between primary and secondary sources in this body of work at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I just don't observe the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I shall primarily be referring to a report that is called the background of the policy and strategies concerning Sarajevo, 91-95.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original title.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. We cannot hear Mr. Lukic because of background noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't -- didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat. I shall repeat. I hope that they hear me now. They did not hear me because of background noise that sometimes occurs when there are several microphones switched on at the same time. So, in your work, did you find documentation itself upon which you based this report, or did somebody offer this to you, or was it a mix of the two?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: A mix of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work in relation to Sarajevo and the siege of Sarajevo, as you call it, did you look at documents of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can that be seen from this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I can't actually recall a specific footnote as you ask that question but it's certainly reflected in many of the statements that are in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you review documents of military units of the SDA, and later, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you review the documents of the MUP, that is to say, the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, in the territory under the control of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I've looked at a few documents from the period prior to 19 -- prior to, let's say, April of 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, you did not look at MUP documents after that period in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although you did not look at military documents, did you have an idea of the strength of the military units in Sarajevo, that is to say, the Muslim military units, as compared to the Serb military units around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you find out? What was the balance of power?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It depended on the time one speaks of. Certainly in 1991, the JNA was much -- far the superior force over any police or military units in Sarajevo, that really continued well into 1992, with the conversion of the JNA to the VRS. At that point I think it started to change. The -- certainly the forces fighting in the name of the government gained recruits, while the VRS was losing them, and also gained some heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned this, now that you said government, I should just like to deal with something very briefly. This government, throughout the war, did it represent all the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the government in Sarajevo represented Serb interests in Bosnia-Herzegovina and abroad? In your view or according to your research?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It had representatives in it of Serbs and at least in their view they were in -- representing the Serb interests in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, they represented Croatian interests after 1993, in your view, after the war broke out between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously much less so after 1993, but, yes, there were those who were in the government who believed they were representing Croatian interests, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about members or representatives in the government who represented Serbs, are you referring to Mirko Pejanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Among others, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the position that Mirko Pejanovic had in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He was a member of the Presidency from about June 1992 until nearly the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that Mirko Pejanovic was not an elected member, that is to say, Serbs never voted for him so that he would be able to represent them; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He competed and won votes in the election of 1990 and was selected based on the number of votes that he received in that election, by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was this position that he was chosen for, selected?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the Presidency, a member of the Presidency. He competed for that position in the November 1990 elections, came in, I believe, third or fourth, something like that, and then when numbers 1 and 2 resigned, he was invited to join the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, he was used by Alija Izetbegovic, right? And the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina never acknowledged that he represented them in any government. In your historical research, would you reach that conclusion, or would you say that the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed to having Mirko Pejanovic represent them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Therefore several questions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to invite Mr. Lukic to split them up. The first question was whether he was used by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know there are those who believe that but I don't believe that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, in your research, actually, did you come across any information to the effect that the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina ever recognised or acknowledged anything that Mirko Pejanovic did as a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The -- Pejanovic and a number of other people formed a Serbian civic council in Sarajevo in 1994, and using that sort of as a formal mechanism, represented the interests of the Serb people, Serbs in the course of the peace talks, first of all, for the Federation and then for Dayton. So, yeah, I think he -- there were -- I know a number of Serbs or could probably name them, if I could come up with the names soon enough, who felt that he was the best representative of the Serb people in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to admit to you that I truly am astonished by such views of yours, but I'm sorry, this is a comment so I shall continue with my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you refrain from such comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to but I really couldn't at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did Mirko Pejanovic do for the five and a half thousand civilians who were killed in Sarajevo, just because they were Serbs? How did he represent their interests?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I -- you've cited a fact that is not in evidence and I don't accept, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I apologise. When you say that it is not in evidence, you mean in this case of ours?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I don't mean in this case. I mean in, let's say, the public domain, in terms of information that is reasonably verified and supported by independent observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I nevertheless try to avoid any confusion? In your question, Mr. Lukic, you refer to five and a half thousand civilians, just because they were Serbs. Now that is first a number and second is the reason why they were killed. Could we split up and see where the witness says that there is no evidence understood as evidence in the public domain? Do you disagree with the number of five and a half thousand and it is suggested by Mr. Lukic that those were Serbs, or is it that you disagree with the fact that if there were five and a half thousand Serbs killed, that it was just because they were Serbs? Could you try to analyse a bit more in detail and to split up the various aspects of the question Mr. Lukic put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the evidence supports that Serbs were killed in Sarajevo because they were Serbs. Or at least because they were engaging in some activity which was judged to be in support of Serbian aims, let's say. I view the number of five and a half thousand as unproven and very likely excessive. There have been some efforts to determine that, and I have to say they have not been particularly successful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when we are talking about Sarajevo -- Mr. Mladic, you know that you are supposed to remain seated. When we are talking about Sarajevo, what are we talking about, the inner city of Sarajevo? I don't know, Mr. Lukic, whether you had any specific geographical reference on your mind when you referred to Sarajevo, area, city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Geographically the territory of the city of Sarajevo under the control of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So not any people that were killed from within the city but died outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because some people consider that to be part of Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe my question wasn't artfully posed but my intention was exactly as you corrected me, that I think only killed on the territory under control of Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Donia says that what he learned from studies is that it's likely an exaggeration to talk about five and a half thousand. If you want to further explore, please go ahead. I'll step out at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I consult with Mr. Mladic for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do it at low volume and short. Otherwise you'll have to wait for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Donia, in view -- in your view, how many Serb civilians were killed in Sarajevo in the territory that was under the control of the Muslim forces, since you are challenging or contesting this figure of five and a half thousand?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know that number. I certainly am aware that a very thorough demographic study was done within the last six, seven years by an agency in Sarajevo that had -- was funded by outside agencies that concluded that the total number killed in Sarajevo during the war was around 10.000. Now, I think it's highly implausible that over 5500 of -- 5500 of those would be Serbs. Some Serbs left at the beginning of the war. Some Muslims left as well, and Croats. But the fact of the matter is that some Serbs were killed because they were Serbs within the territory that you've described as the Muslim territory, and some were killed by the fact that they were simply in the city and under various kinds of assault for those four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, we are yet to have a census in Bosnia-Herzegovina and then we are going to have information that is far more precise. Would you agree with me that the Muslim authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina for years tried to prevent a census of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina from taking place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that already at the beginning of the conflict, the Muslim forces attacked Pofalici, a Serb settlement, and expelled the entire population from it? Of course, except for those who they had killed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm aware of the battle that took place for Pofalici in May of 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talking about Sarajevo, you will agree that it cannot be perceived in isolation but it has to be looked at in the broader context of the events taking place in the region or, rather, in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What gave rise to the tensions that emerged in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Many different factors contributed. Certainly the virtual collapse of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in its socialist version was a part of the causal scene. The arming of factions or paramilitaries under the leadership of various leaders from all three groups contributed to this. The distribution of arms from the JNA to Serb operatives, SDS members and others, in Bosnia contributed. The sharp disagreement over the constitutional future of Bosnia, as we discussed earlier, was a part of that. So deep distrust also contributed, I think, to these tensions in the course of early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the movements for independence in Croatia and Slovenia were a contributing factor to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I would. They contributed in some unexpected ways and some perhaps expected ways, but, yes, they certainly were a factor in that causal scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the arming of paramilitary formations. Would you agree that the first paramilitary formations were set up under the auspices of Alija Izetbegovic's Party of Democratic Action? And I'm talking about the Green Berets and the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. Let me say I think it's difficult to establish who was first in this, and certainly recognise that the Patriotic League and the Green Berets were established no later than June of 1990 and were certainly among the first paramilitaries to operate in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These two formations were a military wing of Alija Izetbegovic's SDA party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. So Yugoslavia broke up, and there was cohesion and links along ethnic lines to a much greater extent than was the case before the war. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I think those links sort of strengthened starting in the very late 1980s and became stronger on the eve of and stronger yet during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at P1999, page 7 in e-court, in English, second paragraph, and also page 7 in the B/C/S version? I asked for page 7 in e-court, not in the report itself. We have it in English, what we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this is what you say: "When we investigate the causes" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot find it in English. You're reading from where exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph, sorry, the second paragraph on this page, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see whether I can -- I don't see the text you're reading. Mr. Lukic, this is page 7 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I'm reading from B/C/S version on the left-hand side and it's same paragraph as in English version, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the English and see whether you can find what you intended to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can read in English, then I can ask my question. "The literature of constructed identity challenges us to consider the mutable, shifting structure of identity in examining the causes and course of violent conflict. I have endeavoured to accept the challenge in this report opening up the casual analysis of events to multiple and contending explanation for the loyalties and identities of Sarajevans in 1990s."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I just correct? You pronounced "causal" as "casual," and there is a difference between the two, but causal analysis of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was in connection only -- the sentence is maybe a bit mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, my question is the following: This annihilation of belonging or allegiance to a certain people, is that what it is? Or do you understand it in some other way? How do you understand it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I view it as a process that is always going on, which changes both the -- occasionally actually loyalty and intensity of loyalty of any given person over time. So this is a specific rejection of the idea that this is an eternal, unchangeable, immutable quality that exists within a person or for that matter that the group, the Serb people, is anything more than an abstraction. Same would be true of the Muslim people or Bosniak people, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, does that mean that the Serbs of Sarajevo were no longer Serbs or was it something there that forced them to give up being Serbs temporarily? Can you provide some more detailed explanation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I accept the notion that ethnicity or a national identity is self-declared, self-determined and self-declared. Consequently, those people who believed themselves to be Serb would presumably identify themselves as Serb in the census and on other occasions. They might well decide at some point in their life that because they were in a mixed marriage or because they no longer wished to be considered a part of the Serb corpus of people, that they declare themselves, for example, as Yugoslavs or as other or as utterly indifferent. I've actually given a couple of examples of that in the course of the report. So do people decide to cease becoming Serbs? Yes, I think so. Some of them, probably the most common movement that I'm speaking about in this period is the migration of those who declared themselves Yugoslavs in 1981, for example, to other specific identities in 1991, and in the opinion of -- that was a consequential shift in the opinion of Serb observers who felt that it was diminishing the number of Serbs and also in the view of Muslim observers who believed that those Yugoslavs were all actually Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your research, did you come across any information as to how many Serbs were forcibly mobilised by the BH Army or how many of them were engaged in digging trenches at the front lines for the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, not any reliable information, or that I would consider as reliable. There were, in fact, many people forced into digging trenches at the front lines. Some of them Serbs, some of them from other groups. But the numbers of them, I have not come across anything that I consider reliable that would tell me how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't deal with that matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's -- I don't think I dealt with that specific issue in this report at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also did not deal with the number of the Serbs killed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I have to say I did do that in an earlier report for another case, but in this particular case, I did not address that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, I'm sorry, but I have to go back to asking you if you reached any conclusion as to how many Serbs were killed in Sarajevo to the extent that you address the issue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is -- I mean, my view is that it is at the very least in the hundreds, probably the high hundreds, and I reached that number simply by looking at the number of prisons that -- into which Serbs were thrown and the type of violence to which they were all subjected, as -- determining the number, as I said, the number, total number of Serbs who died, I think is -- has been studied by the group, I can't think of the name of it, in Sarajevo, that has given to every victim a name, place of death, and an affiliation if possible, and that number, as I said, altogether, is 10.000, give or take a little bit, and that includes, I think, the sense of broader Sarajevo as it existed in 1991. But I don't recall what number they assigned to the total Serb deaths in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. So I'll take it that you did not address the issue of this number. In your research, did you reach any conclusion as to whether the Serbs were free to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I tried. I think it's very difficult to know just exactly what that situation was in the course of the war. Probably changed considerably in the course of the war. My, say, general impression is that it was very easy to get out of Sarajevo, and not only Serbs but members of other groups did it, until May 2nd, roughly speaking, as a dividing line, and thereafter the government made various efforts to limit the exodus of Serb -- or of Sarajevo citizens or inhabitants. Sometimes requiring too much documentation of them, in other cases delaying their departure for a matter of days or weeks. I do have the impression that at the end of the day, you don't have a lot of people craving to get out who did not eventually make it out. That's my general impression. But as I say, there certainly were various restrictions on their departure from at least May 2nd on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say the 2nd of May, you're referring to the 2nd of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the break, tell me, have you heard that the Serbs had to pay some money in order to be allowed to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I have heard that in a few situations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I think it's our time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and a break of 20 minutes. Could Mr. Donia be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I'd like to reserve the last 12, 13 minutes of today's session for a few procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just informing my colleague Ivetic -- he was probably more familiar, not probably, for sure more familiar, than me. So he'll be here for the last 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we please have page 8 in e-court, in the same document that we have on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is your Sarajevo report, doctor. This is about the transformation of the JNA, and you say at the beginning, in the chapter dedicated to the transformation of the Yugoslav People's Army, which -- at the beginning it evolved from its origin into a multi-national force as an instrument of Serb national interests.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to repeat your question for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So is it true that the homogenisation of the JNA occurred because the statutory mobilisation was ignored by members of the Croatian and Muslim ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That would be one of several causes, and probably not the most important one. But certainly did take place, and it had an effect on -- in the direction of homogenising the force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you come across any instructions issued by the Muslim and Croatian authorities telling their compatriots not to respond to the call-up of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: As I recall, I'm sure the instructions that you're referring to didn't really tell them not to join the JNA but sort of gave them permission not to, if they chose to. Those were the instructions of, I think, 30 September 1991 that were issued by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know and did you find in your research that the JNA was also clashing with a Serb armed formation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Very occasionally. I believe I noted one instance of that, if -- I don't think it's in the report but it's in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Not in this one.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next subtitle is, "The JNA's discreet tilt towards nationalism." I'm going to read part of this paragraph so that we know what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Lukic please say where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- but could you also tell the interpreters where you're reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I said the subtitle, "The JNA's discreet tilt towards nationalism" is the subtitle of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has been interpreted, and then you read from where? Same page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second, I'm sorry. [Interpretation] I thought this was immediately beneath the subtitle, but it is actually line 4 in the paragraph right beneath the subtitle, as it begins with, "In addition to bearing responsibility for defending the homeland."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the fifth line of the paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In addition to bearing responsibility for defending the homeland from foreign foes, the force was constitutionally mandated to preserve the internal order of the Federal Socialist Yugoslavia ..." Dr. Donia, would you agree that the army could not possibly ignore their role in preserving the internal order of the state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, they could have, in principle. They certainly did not. They took this mandate very seriously and so behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to take the mandate of preserving a state, be taken not seriously? For example, in the US, is it possible for a policeman to preserve law and order of the country seriously or not seriously?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I would argue that it is possible to do it either way. Hopefully, those in positions of authority take it seriously and implement it, follow it. But is it possible to treat it casually? Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be a matter of language at this moment and not a dispute about -- you wanted to ask whether they were allowed to ignore it, and then I take it your answer would be that they were not allowed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's correct. That would be my answer, they would not be allowed. By whom it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it also true, throughout history, that in a time of crisis, a firmer hand is required, and that when the times are safe and peaceful, the government can act in a more lenient way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Is that true throughout history? No. I wouldn't -- I'd say it's true in most situations at most times but I don't want to make a blanket statement that it's always and forever true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You would agree with me that each and every military officer who failed to carry out his duties must have and should have been the subject of Prosecution by the military judiciary?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Must have and should have? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your paper - we now need page 9, line 3, in the e-court version in English, and also page 9 in B/C/S - this is what you say: "The JNA took measures to prevent its own disintegration along republic borders and strengthening the idea of Yugoslavhood." Would you agree with me that the idea of Yugoslavhood was the strongest in the JNA throughout the existence of Yugoslavia after 1945?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: If I understood your question correct, was the Yugoslav impulse the strongest one after 1945?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, is the strongest one among the members of JNA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to ask you the following: Would you agree that there was no strengthening of that idea that took place? Rather, the same tasks were continued, the same ideas, or, rather, the idea of a common state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: By whom? It's kind of a vague question. Could you ask it -- maybe be more specific about what you're looking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] It is in line of your -- actually, I'm trying to say that your finding here from -- in the third line and further in this page, that the JNA took measures to prevent its own fragmentation along republic lines and strengthen its own fealty to Yugoslavism?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: If that's the question, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Would you also agree that actually those who work against that idea, actually do not accept togetherness?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You would not agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I would not agree with that, yes. I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in your view, separatists are in favour of togetherness? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They can be, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain that to us? I find that to be a bit strange and hard to understand.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think you're responding to your use of the word "togetherness" and I think you're bringing into play the word "separatists" which is very much a political concept as opposed to togetherness which can be social or organisational or anything else. So that's why I responded to your question that separatists can be in favour of togetherness. They may object to the dominant power being too exclusionary and want to restore a sense of togetherness. So the answer to your question is I think I -- I'm not testifying that separatists are inherently in favour of -- either in favour or opposed to togetherness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take you and the witness back to one of the previous questions? You started asking, Mr. Lukic, whether the witness would agree that there was no strengthening of the idea of Yugoslavism and then the witness asked a few things and you suggested that it was not strengthening but just sticking to the same which had been there already. Then you read the portion of the report where those words are used, that is, that the JNA took measures to prevent its own fragmentation along republican lines and strengthen its fealty to Yugoslavism. And then you asked the witness -- then the witness said: "If that is the question, the answer is yes." Now, the question was whether it was rather than strengthening, that it was keeping it on the same level. And after you had read this, I was a bit surprised by the answer that the answer would be yes. Because the portion read clearly says that they were also strengthening Yugoslavism. So it's unclear to me whether you had fully understood the question, or if you had, whether you could explain why despite the language you used, you at the same time answered to the question that there was no strengthening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's largely a matter of what period we are talking about in trying to answer that question. I would point out that in the 1980s, the JNA high command had a lot of discussions about whether to permit the force to fragment or to divide along republic lines, and essentially lay the foundation for, say, what happened in the Soviet Union, which was that the army could, in fact, break into its republican components and as the League of Communists did. They took those measures forcefully to avoid that and at the same time they sought to strengthen the Yugoslav component, the Yugoslav ideology of their organisation, and for that matter, the public loyalty to it. It's a little bit different story when you get into, I would say, 1991, in Croatia, when the army takes a very different turn and then, of course, into Bosnia in 1992 when it eventually divides itself into republic components.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That clarifies the matter for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said just now that they took violent measures to prevent that. Could you actually take a look at line 18 on page 70? When you say they took these measures forcefully and so on, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I did not mean violent. I meant forceful as in decisive measures. I would not allege that they used violence to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These people who were working against the JNA, regardless of whether they were members of the JNA or outside the JNA, were they doing that in order to strengthen or weaken Yugoslavia? What did your research show?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Again, it's a matter of the period in question, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yeah. In 1991, I think they were working to weaken Yugoslavia or at least that part of Yugoslavia that they were a part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although you're not a lawyer, we have established that, in the course of your work, did you come across things like these people being blamed against -- for working against the constitution, against Yugoslavia, that is to say, these people wanting to weaken the JNA and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mention one such incident when the JNA military prosecutors sought to gain punitive measures against the editors of "Mladina" in Slovenia, failed to do so and these defendants sort of emerged as national heroes from that process and the JNA's, let's say, reputation suffered as a product of that, but that's exactly the situation that you described, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should we break at this moment with the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think we need the full 17 minutes but if you would feel --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can continue or whatever you order, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll conclude -- well, we'll not conclude but we will interrupt the cross-examination now. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning, Mr. Donia, at 9.30, in this same courtroom. I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given already or testimony still to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first like to deliver a decision. It is the decision on the Prosecution's motion for leave to add 13 documents related to Witness Turkusic to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list. On the 26th of July, 2013, the Prosecution filed its 92 ter motion in relation to Witness Emir Turkusic, in which it also requested leave to add 13 documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. On the 9th of August, the Defence objected to the motion in its entirety. In accordance with the Chamber's guidance on how the Chamber deals with Rule 92 ter motions on transcript pages 2408 to 2410, the Chamber will decide on the Rule 92 ter motion after the witness has concluded his testimony. Therefore, the Chamber will now address only the request for addition to the Prosecution's exhibit list of the relevant documents, all of which relate to investigations by the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina into shelling incidents in Sarajevo. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution has failed to demonstrate good cause for requesting the addition of these documents at this stage of the proceedings. The Chamber finds, however, that the documents are prima facie relevant and probative of the alleged shelling incidents in Sarajevo charged in the indictment. The Chamber also notes that four of these documents were identified in the original 92 ter motion concerning this witness which was filed on the 25th of January. The remaining nine were identified in the present 92 ter motion filed 30 days in advance of the witness's scheduled testimony. The Chamber considers, therefore, that this has allowed sufficient time for the Defence to process them. This is particularly the case given the relatively short length of the documents which vary between one and six pages in their B/C/S versions. For these reasons, the Chamber finds that the documents' addition to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list will not unduly burden the Defence in the preparation of its case. Consequently, the Chamber finds the addition of documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 29153 to 29165 to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list to be in the interests of justice, and grants this request. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The other matter remaining is -- concerning the report of Mr. Theunens. On the 24th of January of this year, the Chamber requested the Prosecution to correct a number of technical mistakes in the uploading of the report of Mr. Theunens, also to explain the relevance of certain sections of the report and review the report and redact any possible overlap with adjudicated facts. The Prosecution dealt with these matters through filings of the 14th of February of this year, the 15th of July of this year, and the 26th of July. The Chamber therefore considers that the time for the Defence to submit its Rule 94 bis notice is running. The Chamber understands, however, from an informal communication of the 21st of August, 2013, that this has not been clear to the Defence. In the light of this, the Chamber is inclined to grant the Defence two additional weeks, until the 9th of September, 2013, for this submission. That is the matter on the table. Yes, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have one further clarification, Your Honours. The 15th of February, 2013, the Chamber indicated that 180 pages of the Theunens report needed to be revisited whether they are necessary. Do we have a ruling then of the Chamber, are those included or excluded in the report so as to know what to respond to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Prosecution takes the view that they are necessary. Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore still are part of. Is that how I have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's clear, then, as I said, the Chamber is inclined to grant the Defence two additional weeks. They are hereby granted. They have time until the 9th of September of 2013 for the submission under Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said, we would need less than the 17 minutes we had at the time. Mr. Weber, you want to fill the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Not all 17 minutes, Your Honour. But since we are here discussing Witness Theunens, I just wanted to again convey on the record, I know I've done this through e-mail with Mr. Ivetic, but I see in light of the tight turnaround possibly between the notice and then when the witness is testifying that the Prosecution is available, I'm personally available to work through with the Defence in advance of his testimony related to any of the documents or content of the report. I just wanted to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That offer is hereby on the record and is understood by Mr. Ivetic. There being nothing further to be discussed, we adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 23rd of August, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.
